endorsements.quote: Regulators need to require performance testing across subgroups defined by age, language, mobility level, or comorbidities to ensure that performance remains consistent across diverse older adult populations.
Therefore, regulations must establish transparent responsibility frameworks that specify who is responsible for monitoring the system and validating algorithmic outputs.

Because many cognitive monitoring tools function continuously, governance structures should incorporate dynamic and ongoing consent processes to reflect the evolving nature of autonomy in aging populations [ 3 ].

This could involve clearly defined requirements for monitoring subtle changes in algorithm behavior as input patterns evolve, so that systems remain stable and aligned with clinical standards even as they learn from new data.

unlisted_practices: Establish regulatory frameworks that distinguish diagnostic aids used during clinical visits from continuous passive monitoring tools.
Accompany AI-generated alerts with structured workflows that guide clinician responses.
Define when AI-generated notifications of cognitive change should trigger follow-up visits, neuropsychological testing, or additional monitoring.
Use model interpretability tools, standardized validation protocols, and transparent reporting of algorithmic outputs to mitigate epistemic opacity.

screen.reason: This is an editorial discussing ethical challenges and recommending governance frameworks for AI-enabled cognitive monitoring in geriatric care.
